7 [[Big Ten Conference|Western / Big Ten]] (1914–1915, 1918–1919, 1923, 1927–1928) | awards = [[Amos Alonzo Stagg Award]] (1948) | coaching_records = | CFBHOF_year = 1951 | CFBHOF_id = 1412 }} '''Robert Carl Zuppke''' (July 2, 1879 – December 22, 1957) was an [[American football]] coach. He served as the head football coach at the University of Illinois—now known as the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]]–from 1913 until 1941, compiling a record of 131–81–12. Inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 1951, Zuppke coached his teams to [[College football national championships in NCAA Division I FBS|national titles]] in 1914, 1919, 1923, and 1927. Zuppke's teams also won seven [[Big Ten Conference]] championships. Among the players Zuppke coached at Illinois was [[Red Grange]], the era's most celebrated college football player. The field at the University of Illinois's [[Gies Memorial Stadium]] is named Zuppke Field in his honor. Zuppke is credited for many football inventions and traditions, including the [[huddle]] and the [[Flea flicker (American football)|flea flicker]]. In 1914, he reintroduced the [[I formation]].{{Cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OmwfnipKuogC&pg=PA83 | title=The Anatomy of a Game: Football, the Rules, and the Men who Made the Game| isbn=9780874134551| last1=Nelson| first1=David M.| year=1994}} Prior to coaching at the University of Illinois, Zuppke coached at [[Muskegon High School]] in [[Muskegon, Michigan]], and [[Oak Park and River Forest High School]] in [[Oak Park, Illinois]], where he tutored future [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]]r [[George Trafton]] and [[Olympic Games|Olympic]] [[decathlete]] [[Harry Goelitz]].{{Harvnb|Brichford|2009|page=15}} Zuppke led the team to state championships in 1911 and 1912. He had several coaching influences. He used some plays developed by [[Pop Warner]].{{Harvnb|Brichford|2009|page=27}} Zuppke also was a writer and a fine art painter. From 1930 to 1948, Zuppke wrote the syndicated newspaper strip ''Ned Brant'', drawn by [[Walt Depew]].[http://lambiek.net/artists/d/depew_walt.htm DePew bio], Lambiek's Comiclopedia. Accessed December 10, 2011. During the 1930s, Zuppke also wrote syndicated sports-related columns.{{Harvnb|Brichford|2009|p=}} As a painter, Zuppke was known for his rugged Western landscapes. ==Zuppkeisms== Zuppke was given to philosophical remarks, known as "Zuppkeisms." The seven best-known are as follows: # Never let hope elude you; that is life's biggest failure # The greatest athlete is one who can carry a nimble brain to the place of action # Moral courage is the result of respect from fellow men # A good back should keep his feet at all times and never lose his head # Men do their best if they know they are being observed # Alumni are loyal if a coach wins all his games # Advice to freshmen: don't drink the liniment {{cite web |url={{College Football HoF/url|id=1412}} |title=Bob "The Little Dutchman" Zuppke |publisher=[[College Football Hall of Fame]] |access-date=February 17, 2010}} ==Artist== Zuppke was also a painter who worked mainly on creating evocative, naturalistic landscapes depicting the American Southwest. Zuppke saw no conflict between his interest in painting and football strategy as he believed, "Art and football are very much alike".{{cite web|title=Sport: Football Artist|url=http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,758291,00.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120125023423/http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,758291,00.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 25, 2012|date=October 18, 1937|publisher=Time Magazine}} His work was displayed in several shows, including a one-man show at the [[Palmer House Hilton|Palmer House]] in Chicago in 1937. Zuppke was a member of the No-Jury Society of Artists in Chicago and an acquaintance of [[Ernest Hemingway]]. Images of Zuppke alongside some of his paintings can be found in the University of Illinois Archives.{{cite web|title=Robert Zuppke and His Artwork|url=http://www.library.illinois.edu/archives/archon/?p=digitallibrary/digitalcontent&id=3585|publisher=University of Illinois Archives|access-date=December 10, 2011}} ==Head coaching record==
